\chapter{Introduction}
The adverse-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layer is the
canonical flow for studying how pressure forces redistribute
turbulent kinetic energy among the Reynolds stresses.
Wind-tunnel campaigns over the past two decades have mapped the
response of the outer layer to increasingly strong gradients,
yet the budget terms themselves remain sparsely documented.

This thesis reanalyses three stations from a recent campaign
and assembles the full stress budgets at each station.

\section{Equilibrium Estimates}
At station three the boundary layer is close to equilibrium,
and the wake strength is nearly constant across the traverse.
The Clauser parameter $\betta = 1.6$ at this station indicates a
moderate adverse pressure gradient, and the stress profiles
collapse reasonably well on outer variables.

A local-equilibrium argument then closes the budget:
production balances dissipation in the overlap layer,
and the remaining terms are estimated from the measured profiles.

\chapter{Measured Budget Terms}
The measured production and dissipation profiles agree with the
equilibrium estimate to within the calibration uncertainty.
The pressure--strain term is inferred as the closing entry
and shows the expected transfer toward the wall-normal component.

These results support the climbing-wall scaling over the
central portion of the layer and motivate the finer
near-wall measurements proposed in the final chapter.
